documentation.title: Design
documentation.value:
## Overview

This part encodes BoPep4, a 23-residue plant elicitor peptide (PEP) from broccoli (*Brassica oleracea var. italica).*

The part is a translational fusion with three elements, in this order:

1. **SamyQ signal peptide (BBa\_K1074014):** N-terminal signal peptide of the amyQ gene, which encodes a highly efficient α-amylase natively found in Bacillus subtilis (and related lineages like Bacillus amyloliquefaciens). Csn and SamyQ were selected as candidates to determine which signal peptide offers higher secretion efficiency.
2. **Bopep4 Δ 15-23 (**[BBa\_26YHOQCL](https://registry.igem.org/parts/bba-26yhoqcl)**):** encodes BoPep4, a 23-residue plant elicitor peptide (PEP) from broccoli (*Brassica oleracea var. italica)*. In this version of BoPep4, residues 15–23 were deleted.
3. **6x Histag:** fused N-terminally to the peptide. This allows detection and quantification of the short peptide after successful assembly and electroporation.

The complete part was obtained by de novo gene synthesis.

## **About**

* **Biosafety level:** S1 
* **Target organism:** *Bacillus subtilis* \[168 / WB800]
* **Main purpose of use:** negative control for the truncation series. It is the nine C-terminal residues, chosen because the AtPep1 literature shows activity collapses at this length. Any positive result is only meaningful with a construct that should fail sitting next to it.
* **Potential application:** 
  * A cheap second negative control in a dose-response assay, alongside every reported positive.
  * A benchmark for testing whether simulation acceptance criteria can separate binders from non-binders, since it passed a checklist it was expected to fail.
  * A guide to the minimal active region of BoPep4, for designing shorter variants.

## Literature

**Why we built it**

**A positive result is only worth as much as the control next to it.** Our truncation series needed one construct that should not work, so that the constructs that do work mean something. BoPep4 15–23 is that construct. It was ordered to fail.

**The literature chose the fragment for us.** Pearce and colleagues ran exactly this experiment on AtPep1, the Arabidopsis peptide BoPep4 is modelled on. Removing residues from the N-terminus barely changed activity down to AtPep1(9–23) — but activity was completely abolished when nine C-terminal amino acids remained. BoPep4 15–23 **is** those nine residues. The smallest fragment still active in their hands was 14–23, one residue longer. So the cut point is not arbitrary: it is one residue past a measured activity cliff, on the peptide family our part belongs to.

**Our own docking agreed before we ran anything.** We docked the whole ladder — 1–23 down to 17–23, 17 peptides against the PEPR1 ectodomain — with two independent methods. 15–23 sits at the bottom of both: a HADDOCK score of -97.8 kcal/mol against -197.8 for the wild type, and an AlphaFold3 interface confidence of 0.63 against 0.82. Figure T-1.

**What it keeps, and what it gives up**

This is where the construct stopped being routine. 15–23 keeps **all eight** of the crystallographic contacts Tang and colleagues identified, and 49.8 % of the total contact occupancy our wild-type simulation measures. What it loses is everything the N-terminal half was doing: **17 receptor partners** at 50 % occupancy or better, 5 of them tyrosines, and two salt bridges that are present in almost every frame of the wild-type run — Arg9–Asp179 at 99.3 % and Lys7–Asp129 at 96.4 %. Figure T-2.

So the fragment was expected to sit in the groove by its C-terminal anchor and fall out, because half the interface that holds it there is gone.

**What we predicted, and what happened**

The prediction was written into the simulation notebook before the run, and we are quoting it unchanged: 

*“The acceptance criteria are EXPECTED TO FAIL here. That is the result, not an error.”*

**Four of four passed.** Over 30 ns, 15–23 held the Asn23–Arg487 salt bridge for 99.9 % of frames and full clamp integrity for 99.9 % — against 100.0 % and 100.0 % for the full-length wild type. Its peptide RMSD, 1.83 Å, is lower than the wild type's 2.77 Å. By every measure we had written down, the negative control is indistinguishable from the molecule it was meant to be the opposite of. Figures T-3 and T-4.

**What we take from it — and what we do not claim**

**We are not claiming 15–23 is active.** Pearce measured the AtPep1 equivalent as inactive, and we have no activity data of our own on BoPep4. A peptide can stay in a groove for 30 ns and still be a poor binder; residence on this timescale is not affinity.

**What the run does establish is about our method, and it is the more useful result.** A 30 ns simulation scored on a contact checklist measures whether a modelled pose is self-consistent — not whether a peptide binds. The checklist had eight contacts on it, 15–23 keeps all eight, and so the checklist cannot separate it from the wild type. The 17 partners and two salt bridges it loses were never on the list. The negative control did its job by failing to fail: it showed us the limits of our own acceptance criteria before we read anything into them.

**This also reframes the rest of the panel.** The ordered minimal construct 9–23 is the weakest system we simulated at pH 7 (Arg487 81.1 %, clamp 77.1 %), weaker than the fragment we built to be dead. Any ranking of these constructs by simulation alone should be treated as untested until a dose–response measures them.

**What would settle it:** a dose–response assay. 15–23 is cheap to include and, if the literature transfers, it is a free second negative control for every positive we report.

## Dry lab / computational analysis



![](https://registry.igem.wiki/documentation/ee99915c-c6fa-4df0-9249-53c418ad9dc6/c0ae657fc1d1f7ccbee27e8f44d6535bb0f4bdffa9f32e1e20c8539c3aca25fc.avif)

**Figure 1. Where 15–23 sits in the truncation ladder.** Every N-terminal truncation of BoPep4 from 1–23 to 17–23 docked against the PEPR1 ectodomain by two independent methods: AlphaFold3 interface confidence (ipTM, green, left axis) and HADDOCK score (grey, right axis; more negative is better). 15–23 is circled in red: HADDOCK -97.8 kcal/mol and ipTM 0.63, against -197.8 and 0.82 for the wild type. The background shading marks what Pearce and colleagues measured on the equivalent AtPep1 fragments — active down to 14–23, inactive at 15–23 and shorter. Two honest notes. The ipTM minimum falls at 14–23, which is the shortest **active** fragment in Pearce's hands, so the computed cliff and the measured cliff do not land on the same residue. And no ipTM value was returned for 2–23, which is why the green line is broken there. Docking ranks engagement, not affinity; it was used here to choose where to sample the ladder, not to predict potency.



![](https://registry.igem.wiki/documentation/ee99915c-c6fa-4df0-9249-53c418ad9dc6/a1dda76e26ac032ee68efd1155252378488f110b5473999adfbb0f0e2cb0577a.avif)

**Figure 2. 15–23 keeps every checklist contact and gives up half the interface.** (a) Total contact occupancy contributed by each BoPep4 residue, summed over all receptor residues, measured on the 30 ns wild-type trajectory. Residues 1–14, lost in this construct, are red; residues 15–23, retained, are teal. (b) The ledger. 15–23 retains 49.8 % of total contact occupancy and all eight of the crystallographic contacts, but loses 17 receptor partners at 50 % occupancy or better — 5 of them tyrosines — and two near-permanent salt bridges, Arg9–Asp179 (99.3 % of frames) and Lys7–Asp129 (96.4 %). The Asn23 carboxylate–Arg487 salt bridge, present in 100 % of wild-type frames, is retained. Receptor residues are in the original PEPR1 numbering. This is the structural reason the construct was expected to fail: the anchor survives, the shelf that holds the peptide against the groove does not.



![](https://registry.igem.wiki/documentation/ee99915c-c6fa-4df0-9249-53c418ad9dc6/c8817e5e189a17a9f7d0e8fff92cf2352cfe30231dd8a1bc9c9aab45c9867fff.avif)

**Figure 3. The negative control behaves like the wild type.** Four systems over 30 ns, 1,500 frames each, smoothed with a 500 ps rolling average for legibility. (a) Receptor backbone movement. (b) Peptide movement measured in the receptor's frame, so the trace reports displacement within the groove rather than the peptide's own flexibility. (c) Shortest heavy-atom distance across the Asn23–Arg487 salt bridge. (d) Clamp integrity, the number of the four defining contacts made per frame. In (c) and (d) the 15–23 trace (teal) lies on top of the wild type (green) for the whole run, while the ordered 9–23 construct (orange) repeatedly opens and closes. Dotted lines are the pre-registered acceptance gates. OpenMM 8, AMBER ff19SB, OPC water, 0.15 M NaCl, full 710-residue PEPR1 ectodomain, about 127,000 atoms, single run per system.



![](https://registry.igem.wiki/documentation/ee99915c-c6fa-4df0-9249-53c418ad9dc6/6f90097d0ba9368d52fc2b67a5266963d78f4661ff939a11ab4ce799b2e263ac.avif)

**Figure 4. What we predicted against what we measured.** The four acceptance criteria were written down before the simulation ran, together with the explicit prediction that this construct would fail all of them. It passed all four: receptor Cα RMSD 2.10 Å, peptide backbone RMSD 1.83 Å, Asn23–Arg487 within 4 Å for 99.9 % of frames, and clamp integrity at or above 3 of 4 for 100.0 %. We report this as the result rather than adjusting the criteria afterwards. The criteria were not wrong about the chemistry — they were measuring something other than binding.

## **References**

**1.**  Pearce, G., Yamaguchi, Y., Munske, G. & Ryan, C. A. (2008) Structure-activity studies of AtPep1, a plant peptide signal involved in the innate immune response. Peptides 29, 2083-2089.  doi:10.1016/j.peptides.2008.08.019  *— the measured activity cliff; the nine-residue fragment is inactive*

**2.**  Tang, J., Han, Z., Sun, Y., Zhang, H., Gong, X. & Chai, J. (2015) Structural basis for recognition of an endogenous peptide by the plant receptor kinase PEPR1. Cell Research 25, 110-120.  doi:10.1038/cr.2014.161  *— PDB 5GR8; the eight contacts and the Asn23-Arg487 salt bridge*

**3.**  Wang, A., Guo, J., Wang, S., Zhang, Y., Lu, F., Duan, J., Liu, Z. & Ji, W. (2022) BoPEP4, a C-terminally encoded plant elicitor peptide from broccoli, plays a role in salinity stress tolerance. International Journal of Molecular Sciences 23, 3090.  doi:10.3390/ijms23063090  *— BoPep4 itself*

**4.**  Abramson, J. et al. (2024) Accurate structure prediction of biomolecular interactions with AlphaFold3. Nature 630, 493-500.  doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07487-w  *— the ipTM values in Figure T-1*

**5.**  Dominguez, C., Boelens, R. & Bonvin, A. M. J. J. (2003) HADDOCK: a protein-protein docking approach based on biochemical or biophysical information. Journal of the American Chemical Society 125, 1731-1737.  doi:10.1021/ja026939x  *— the HADDOCK scores in Figure T-1*

**6.**  Eastman, P., Galvelis, R., Pelaez, R. P. et al. (2024) OpenMM 8: molecular dynamics simulation with machine learning potentials. Journal of Physical Chemistry B 128, 109-116.  doi:10.1021/acs.jpcb.3c06662  *— the MD engine*

**7.**  Tian, C., Kasavajhala, K., Belfon, K. A. A. et al. (2020) ff19SB: amino-acid-specific protein backbone parameters trained against quantum mechanics energy surfaces in solution. Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation 16, 528-552.  doi:10.1021/acs.jctc.9b00591  *— the protein force field*

**8.**  Izadi, S., Anandakrishnan, R. & Onufriev, A. V. (2014) Building water models: a different approach. Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters 5, 3863-3871.  *— the OPC water model*

**9.** Li, R., Liu, M., Hu, X., Li, J., Pang, Q., Yan, X., Li, J., & Ji, W. (2026). Broccoli plant elicitor peptide BoPep4 enhances plant salt tolerance by improving glucosinolate metabolism. *Plant Science, 364, 112954.*

documentation.title: Application
documentation.value:
This part was designed for the GEMS-Taiwan 2026 iGEM team’s work on a Stress-Responsive Optogenetic Bioreactor for Precision Plant Protection and is used in the construction of the composite part:

* **Pveg-EEBD-RBS0-SamyQ-Bopep4 Δ 15-23-Histag-B0015** ([BBa\_26Z8FHTR](https://registry.igem.org/parts/bba-26z8fhtr)): this Protectant Module constitutively expresses potential stress-mitigation proteins and enables evaluation of their secretion and detection, with its constitutive promoter Pveg, RBS EEBD-RBS0, and terminator B0015.
